newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Renewed probe into scandal hits S.Korean markets.
newsitem.headline: Renewed probe into scandal hits S.Korean markets.

text.p: The reopening of a probe into the loans scandal surrounding failed Hanbo Steel Co rattled South Korean financial markets on Monday, pushing the currency to a seven-year low and shaving stock prices.

Dealers and analysts said the move by state prosecutors stirred fears that a hoped-for economic recovery would be delayed as banks may try to head off further corporate failures by tightening credit to discourage corporate investment.

Prosecutors said at the weekend that it would reinvestigate the collapse in January of Hanbo Steel and look into rumours that President Kim Young-sam's son took a 200 billion won ($226 million) kickback from a Hanbo deal.
Kim Hyun-chul, the president's second son, is already at the heart of a parliamentary inquiry into the collapse of Hanbo Steel under debts totalling $5.8 billion.

"The probe is, and will be, the main factor affecting the market for the time being," said Koh Kyung-bae, an analyst at brokerage Hyundai Securities. "The news came as many investors began to think the scandal is over."
An earlier probe into the scandal led to arrests and trials of 10 people, including a cabinet minister, top bankers and senior politicians, on charges of bribery.
But the political opposition has termed the earlier probe a whitewash that obscured complicity at the highest levels, and has demanded a new investigation.

A state banking watchdog said banks had given loans to Hanbo Steel despite insufficient collateral and the company's poor prospects. Prosecutors said bank officials would be questioned on whether they had received kickbacks from Hanbo in return.

The won hit 887.90 to the dollar, a seven-year intraday low, early on Monday and ended at 887.80, its lowest closing rate since Seoul introduced a market average system in March 1990. That compared with Friday's close of 884.90.
The central bank said it would supply $1 billion to local banks to ease a dollar shortage, but dealers said the announcement had little immediate impact on the market.

On the Seoul bourse, the leading stock index fell 2.45 percent to an intraday low of 607.87 in the morning before clawing back on bargain hunting of banking and blue-chip shares to close at 617.26, down 0.94 percent from Saturday.
"The basic sentiment remains weak," said Park Byung-moon, research manager at LG Securities.
The fall of the local currency, which has lost about 12 percent to the dollar since the start of 1996, came despite forward-trading intervention by the Bank of Korea, dealers said.
They said the bank's offers to sell about $300 million in the three- and six-month forward trading were quickly absorbed by the market.
"The won is likely to weaken further, given the country's economic woes," a domestic bank dealer said.

The won had already been pressured by the country's current account deficit, which widened to $3.09 billion in January from a shortfall of $1.89 billion in the year-earlier month. The government has set a target of reducing the annual deficit to about $18 billion this year from $23.72 billion in 1996.

The collapses of Hanbo Steel in January and Sammi Steel Co last week, together with weeks of labour strikes in January, have stoked fears of further bankruptcies and dashed hopes for an economic revival.
Finance Minister Kang Kyong-shik said the nation should brace for economic growth of only about five percent this year, against rises of 7.1 percent last year and 8.9 percent in 1995.
